Abstract
The subject’s psychological and cognitive activities are important interdisciplinary issues in psychology, cognitive science, and philosophy. The Chinese philosophy of information innovatively provides a philosophical definition of the concepts of subject and object from the dimension of information activity, while also making specific provisions for the cognitive activities of the subject. The subject’s psychology and cognition are an activity of advanced grasping and creation of information. The subject’s information activities have five basic levels. Arranged from lower to higher, they are: the subject’s in-itself information activities, the subject’s intuitive discernment of information, the subject’s memory storage of information, the subject’s subjective creation of information, and the subject’s practice and social realization of information. Higher-level information activities must arise on the basis of lower-level ones. Therefore, the emergence and development of the subject’s psychology and cognition necessarily constitute a highly integrated and complex process of information activities.
1 Introduction
In recent years, research on cognition and psychological issues has increasingly tended toward integrative approaches. Frontier explorations across multiple disciplines—including cognitive science, neurophilosophy, psychology, information science, and the Chinese philosophy of information—converge on a core issue: the subject’s interpretation of information and psychological construction is not a single linear process, but rather a complex system characterized by distinct multi-level and highly integrative features. In the area of integrated information research spanning cognition, neural activity, and psychology, Nartallo-Kaluarachchi and colleagues through multi-level irreversibility analysis of brain dynamics, confirmed the existence of nonlinear hierarchical interactions between sensory and cognitive brain regions in information processing (
Nartallo-Kaluarachchi et al., 2025
). Kagan, starting from information-processing capacity, constructed a quantifiable hierarchical framework ranging from reactive memoryless systems to adaptive, self-regulating agents, thereby providing necessary information-based conditions for identifying “agency” (
Kagan et al., 2025
). Meanwhile, digital technologies are reshaping the subject’s identity structure, emphasizing a mode of existence based on multi-level information integration. Kovalenko points out that the contemporary subject’s information interpretation has evolved into a distributed, hypertextual form of self-construction (
Kovalenko, 2025
). Wu, from the perspective of information ontology, summarizes the multiple identities of the subject’s existence, transcendence, and evolution (
Wu, 2023
). Thus, whether in everyday cognition, technology-assisted activities, or neural activity, the subject continuously interacts with the information environment at different levels and hierarchies. It is precisely this ubiquitous multi-level complex structure that leads us back to the classical division of information forms in the Chinese philosophy of information—in-itself information, for-itself information, and regenerated information. This division reveals a complete evolutionary path of information from objective indirect existence, through the subject’s intuitive grasping, to symbolic creation and re-creation, providing a solid epistemological foundation for understanding the multi-level structure of the subject’s psychology and cognition.
2 The informational essence of cognition and psychology
Since Descartes, modern philosophy has closely tied the concept of the “subject” to “consciousness.” Descartes, through his cogito, ergo sum, defined the subject as a “thinking substance” capable of thinking, doubting, understanding, affirming, denying, willing, imagining, and sensing. Kant elevated the subject to a transcendental level, arguing that the subject actively synthesizes sensuous intuitions
a priori
through the categories of understanding, thereby constituting the objects of knowledge. Husserl’s phenomenology, centered on “intentionality,” posits that consciousness is always “consciousness of something.” Sartre further distinguished “being-in-itself” from “being-for-itself,” pointing out that “for-itself” is precisely the essential determination of the subject—it is never what it is, but always transcends itself, negates the given, and creates the future. In this traditional sense, the “subject” is an entity whose essence is consciousness and freedom.
